summary: On 5 December, German attacks falter and Konev’s troops begin the counteroffensive. Moscow, Tikhvin and the southern front show the failure of a short-war strategy amid continuing occupation and civilian danger.
body:
The end of an expectation

On the morning of 5 December 1941, Heinz Guderian still hoped to complete the encirclement of Tula. By evening, the commander of Second Panzer Army was proposing to pull his exposed forces back toward the Don and Shat rivers. The change did not represent a sudden discovery that winter existed. It followed repeated failures to eliminate Tula, Soviet pressure against the army's extended positions, and the declining ability of its troops and vehicles to continue offensive operations. One of the commanders most closely associated with German armoured warfare was now trying to preserve the force that had been sent around Moscow's southern flank.[1]

Farther north, Soviet troops of Ivan Konev's Kalinin Front were beginning counteroffensive operations. The broader attacks associated with the Moscow counteroffensive would develop from 6 December, with different armies entering the fighting at different times. There was no single instant when an entire front turned around. German attacks had continued while Soviet counterattacks were already taking place, and preparations for wider operations had overlapped with the immediate effort to contain dangerous penetrations. The transition was a process experienced unevenly by armies separated by hundreds of kilometres.[1]

Ostkrieg ends this phase on 5 December as an editorial boundary, not a universally agreed formal termination of Barbarossa. The invasion had failed to destroy the Soviet state’s capacity for sustained resistance. Moscow remained under Soviet control, Leningrad had not surrendered and Soviet forces had recovered Rostov. German armies nevertheless occupied enormous territories and retained the power to kill, imprison and prepare further operations. The campaign’s failure must be assessed on both scales. It was a fundamental defeat of Germany’s expectation of a short war; it did not deliver immediate safety to the people living under occupation or behind the front.[1][2]

The final study brings the separate theatres together at that boundary. Around Moscow, the remaining German attacks were exhausting themselves as the Soviet command prepared a broader response. At Tikhvin, Soviet pressure was increasing but the town remained in German hands. In the south, the Germans had retreated from Rostov while retaining much of their conquered position. The explanatory question is what connected these different outcomes. Soviet forces continued to exist, reinforce and act; German commanders could no longer make their available strength serve all the purposes assigned to it. Those relationships, rather than one city or one temperature, explain the failure of the campaign.[1][3]

Moscow: a counteroffensive in stages

The German position around Moscow had become a collection of exposed advances rather than an effective encirclement. Third Panzer Group, commanded by Georg-Hans Reinhardt, had reached the canal approaches northeast of the capital but could not turn that achievement into a secure advance southward. Erich Hoepner's Fourth Panzer Group was checked on the northwestern approaches. Günther von Kluge's Fourth Army had gone over to the defensive after its latest attempt to break through farther south. Guderian's army remained extended around an undefeated Tula. These formations faced different immediate problems, but all depended on a degree of mutual support that the campaign had failed to produce.[1]

Zhukov's orders gave the counterattack concrete geographical aims. In the north, blows toward Klin, Solnechnogorsk and Istra were intended to dislocate the advanced German wing. In the south, the targets included Uzlovaya and Bogoroditsk, behind Guderian's extended formations. Recovering roads and junctions could compel withdrawals from positions closer to Moscow without storming every defended locality in succession. The orders still had to be executed by armies of uneven strength, and their objectives were not accomplished facts on 5 December. They show the intended answer to the German advance: attack the flanks and communications that made its forward positions sustainable.[1]

Georgy Zhukov's Western Front possessed new opportunities, but its forces had not assembled in ideal conditions. Vasily Kuznetsov's First Shock Army had already been committed near the canal. Dmitry Lelyushenko's Thirtieth Army was positioned to threaten the northern side of the German advance. The Twentieth Army was entering the battle on the approaches between them and the established defenders, while Konstantin Rokossovsky's Sixteenth Army had borne prolonged pressure farther west. The existence of these headquarters did not mean that every assigned unit had arrived, completed its preparation, or received the transport needed for a sustained pursuit.[1]

The opening developed through different fronts and dates. On 5 December, Twenty-Ninth Army troops crossed the frozen Volga west of Kalinin and gained a limited penetration before being stopped. Zhukov issued Western Front’s order that day for the broader attack on the 6th; Sixteenth Army’s principal effort followed on the 7th. To the southeast, Third and Thirteenth armies had been ordered to attack German Second Army from 6 December toward Yefremov and beyond Yelets toward Livny. These later starts clarify the transition without extending this study into the winter campaign’s results. On the 5th, instructions and initial action still exceeded the success already achieved.[1]

Konev had objected that Kalinin Front lacked enough tanks and infantry. Vasilevsky travelled to his headquarters during the night of 4 December with the instruction to begin the following day. The U.S. Army account draws on later Soviet command narratives, whose certainty must not be projected backward into the decision. The objection establishes that the attack was ordered amid acknowledged weakness. Waiting offered time to assemble, but also time for the Germans to regroup and defend their exposed positions. The Soviet command chose to attack during that vulnerable interval. The limited first penetration shows how much remained to be won after the order was given.[1]

The northern war beyond Moscow

Army Group North's position shows why the campaign cannot be understood solely from the approaches to the Soviet capital. Wilhelm von Leeb's forces continued to maintain the blockade of Leningrad while their advance toward Tikhvin had created another exposed commitment. Tikhvin mattered because its railway lay within the transport system supporting the Ladoga approaches. German possession threatened supply arrangements for the besieged city and offered the prospect of extending pressure eastward. Holding that advanced position, however, required troops and supplies that were also needed elsewhere along the army group's broad front.[1]

Kirill Meretskov's Fourth Independent Army had been fighting to reverse the German advance during November. Its early efforts had limited reinforcement and did not produce an immediate liberation of the town. By 5 December, regrouping and additional forces enabled Meretskov to exert pressure toward Tikhvin from three sides. This was a change in the local balance, achieved through continued preparation and combat. It did not mean that Tikhvin was already back in Soviet hands on the date of this chapter, or that Leningrad's blockade had been lifted.[1][4]

Leeb feared that a reduced threat to Moscow would free further Soviet forces for the northern battle. His own advance toward Lake Ladoga had already been stopped near Volkhov on 1 December. German air reconnaissance reported twenty-nine trains moving west along the Vologda–Tikhvin line the next day, a reported movement that heightened concern about reinforcement rather than proving the contents of every train. The intended link with Finnish forces had still not been achieved. Soviet activity around Tikhvin therefore threatened both a vulnerable salient and the larger German hope of tightening the isolation of Leningrad from the east.[1][4]

The food crisis inside Leningrad was already severe. From 20 November, the basic daily bread allowance was 250 grams for workers and engineering staff and 125 grams for employees, dependants and children, as quoted from the decree in the Presidential Library’s account. Those were entitlements, not proof that every recipient obtained a complete ration on time, and bread weight alone does not establish a full diet. The distinctions between categories mattered to households trying to survive. They also connect the fighting over Tikhvin to an immediate civilian deadline: a transport route would have to carry usable supplies before military success could relieve hunger.[11]

A birthday measured in food

Lena Mukhina spent her seventeenth birthday, 21 November, ill in bed. Her diary records 125 grams of bread and 200 grams of sweets that she intended to spread over ten days. She had already eaten more sweets than the plan allowed and recalculated what would remain. This is the experience of one household, preserved in an edited diary extract. Its force lies in the choices it records: the desire to mark a birthday, the pleasure of eating and the knowledge that food consumed now would be missing later. A daily ration had become a calculation extending into every expectation of the next day.[5]

The south after Rostov

The southern theatre had already supplied a clear German reverse. The Rostov counteroffensive forced First Panzer Army away from the lower Don and helped precipitate Gerd von Rundstedt's dismissal. By early December, however, Army Group South had established a defensible position farther west along the Mius and Donets system. Walter von Reichenau, Rundstedt's replacement, had accepted the need for withdrawal once he confronted the operational circumstances. The retreat removed an exposed advance; it did not erase the army group's earlier conquests.[1][2]

Sixth Army retained Kharkov, Belgorod, and Oboyan on the army group's northern side. Seventeenth Army and First Panzer Army held positions across the western Donbas and toward the Mius. These were territories of industrial, agricultural, and transport importance, with populations living under German occupation. Soviet recovery of Rostov had frustrated an immediate German approach toward the Caucasus and improved the southern strategic position, but it had not recovered the whole Donbas or placed every German formation in retreat. The map remained a record of both Soviet resistance and extensive German territorial power.[2]

In Crimea, Erich von Manstein's Eleventh Army confronted another failure to turn an advance into the elimination of organised resistance. Sevastopol remained in Soviet hands. Ivan Petrov's Independent Maritime Army, reinforced by men evacuated from Odessa, had helped prevent the fortress from being overrun in early November. Naval gunfire and supply by sea supported the defence. Under Filipp Oktyabrsky, the Sevastopol Defence Region had strengthened its landward positions during November, while rain delayed the next organised German assault. The city's continued resistance tied down forces and preserved a Soviet base within the peninsula.[2]

The German position at Tikhvin was also still unresolved. Soviet forces had increased the pressure, and the town would be recovered on 9 December after the German decision to withdraw. That later outcome must not be counted as a victory already achieved on the 5th, still less as the end of Leningrad’s siege. Across the three army groups, failure had different visible forms: abandoned ground at Rostov, a threatened salient at Tikhvin and frustrated attacks before Moscow. The common result was the loss of a credible short-war solution, while the invading armies retained enough strength and territory to continue a devastating conflict.[2][4]

Why resources no longer matched objectives

German resources had been consumed through the campaign itself. Casualties removed trained men; vehicle wear reduced transport; the extension of occupied territory enlarged the work of supply and security. The November decision to attack made these pressures more immediate. Infantry and vehicles still needed for another advance were also needed to bring forward winter equipment and prepare defensible positions. Bock’s late argument for retaining the initiative acknowledged the predicament: his weakened troops already occupied ground difficult to hold. Continuing to attack delayed the transition while spending resources that the transition would require.[6][1]

Guderian's position showed how attack and withdrawal competed for the same diminishing resources. His advanced troops needed fuel to move out of the bulge around Tula, just as they had needed it to close the encirclement. Soviet attacks northeast of Venev threatened the flank and rear of formations already suffering from mechanical failures and restricted movement. Pulling back could shorten their exposure, but the retreat had to begin while they could still move their equipment and maintain contact. By the evening of 5 December, preserving the army had become more urgent than completing the operation that had carried it into those positions.[7][1]

Soviet survival rested on institutions capable of continuing to raise forces and sustain resistance after enormous losses. Industrial evacuation contributed to that capacity, but its effects must be placed on the correct timescale. Mark Harrison's research emphasises the disruption involved in moving factories and their workforces, the differences in how quickly enterprises resumed production, and the improvisation required at receiving sites. Removing machinery from the enemy's path preserved a possibility; buildings, power, labour, and supply connections still had to make that possibility productive. The later achievements of Soviet industry should not be projected backward as if they were fully available in November.[3]

David Glantz places Soviet reinforcement in a wider institutional setting. His survey identifies ten additional field armies raised during November and December, with several committed around Moscow during the defence or the winter operations that followed. This is a two-month process, not a reserve total already available on 5 December. The new armies were often deficient in the equipment and supporting organisation required by Soviet doctrine. Their importance was that the state could continue assembling them after losing so much of its pre-war force. Glantz also treats the winter counteroffensive as successive operations rather than one simultaneous blow. That interpretation helps reconcile Soviet recovery with the incomplete arrivals and limited opening attacks recorded at individual fronts: new military strength was real, but its deployment and effect unfolded unevenly.[8]

A comparison with unequal denominators

The U.S. Army history compares Soviet publications giving approximately 1.7 million German and 1.1 million Soviet personnel before the counteroffensive. It warns that their coverage differs: the German total includes Army Group Centre and associated air personnel, while the Soviet figure covers the attacking fronts and omits the Stavka reserve. These are retrospective published estimates, not matching strength returns inspected here. They establish the scale of the armies but cannot yield a reliable local superiority ratio. A division’s condition, the reserves available to its commander and the troops concentrated at an actual crossing mattered more directly to that crossing’s battle.[1]

Judgement, weather, and human responsibility

Bock’s intelligence judgement remained wrong even after he had recognised his own army’s exhaustion. On 4 December he treated reported Soviet reinforcements northwest of Moscow as transfers from quiet sectors and told the army high command that a counteroffensive was unlikely because the opponent lacked the forces. The following day Konev attacked. This is a more precise failure than a general statement that German intelligence knew nothing. Headquarters received indications of additional troops, but interpreted them within an expectation of Soviet depletion. Recognition of German weakness did not produce an adequate estimate of Soviet remaining capability.[1]

Cold aggravated the resulting danger. It reduced vehicle reliability, complicated the use of weapons and inflicted casualties on inadequately equipped men. The operational record already showed severe losses and failed attacks before the final temperature drop. Soviet resistance had held Tula, checked Hoepner and contested the canal; German decisions had left exhausted formations in exposed positions. Winter increased the cost of that predicament rather than creating all of it. Soviet troops also had to move and fight in the cold. Their success required using the opportunity through organised action, with losses and difficulties that a climatic explanation alone would conceal.[1][6]

German treatment of prisoners demonstrates why exposure cannot be separated from policy. Reinhard Otto cites a German inspection of the Michailowski prisoner collecting point in Belarus dated 1 December: it held more than 10,000 Soviet soldiers, and 144 had died the preceding night. The inspector described food as wholly insufficient; men classed as unable to work received still less than working prisoners. These are the report’s figures for one camp and one night, reproduced in Otto’s scholarship, not a total for the Moscow battle. They identify an institutional choice with lethal consequences. The weakest captives were given the least support, deepening the condition that had made them unable to work.[12]

The Soviet defence also imposed destructive choices on civilians. The 17 November shelter-denial order and the reported burning of settlements are examined in The Southern Pincer. They belong to a history in which preserving the Soviet state could protect communities from occupation while the state’s own military measures destroyed homes and compelled displacement. The German and Soviet policies require distinct accounts of purpose, implementation and responsibility. Neither a common language of winter hardship nor the eventual outcome of the war resolves those differences. The people deprived of shelter needed warmth immediately, whatever strategic advantage a headquarters expected from the deprivation.[9]

Hunger was likewise changing what Leningrad’s residents could physically do. In his entries of 6–7 November, Yura Ryabinkin described difficulty studying and exhaustion after carrying rubbish downstairs and climbing back to the family’s flat. The observation is individual and earlier than the concluding date, but it explains why improved supply could not be measured solely in tonnes dispatched. Food had to reach people whose capacity to queue, carry water and care for others was deteriorating. Recovery of a railway connection and recovery of a household’s strength were related processes with different timescales. The fighting outside Leningrad had not ended that emergency by 5 December.[5]

A war that would continue

Diplomatic correspondence supplies another measure of the unfinished war. In November, American officials were still arranging shipping and aircraft assembly to meet commitments to the Soviet Union, while Soviet representatives pressed for faster assistance and a stronger British diversion. Those exchanges record decisions, complaints and preparations; they do not provide a delivery inventory for the armies defending Moscow. Their significance at the phase’s close was that a continuing Soviet war made continuing assistance possible. The defenders had preserved the state and communications to which the emerging coalition could direct help.[10]

That future had remained open through costly decisions in the present. Zhukov committed newly assembling armies while retaining forces needed for defence; Cherevichenko redirected his offensive after Rostov fell; Meretskov rebuilt pressure on Tikhvin without an immediate victory. These were distinct operations, and none guaranteed the others. Their combined effect was to confront Germany with an opponent still able to organise new action across the front. The invasion had inflicted catastrophic losses without preventing that recovery. The explanation lies in Soviet decisions and institutions surviving those losses, and in German forces becoming less able to interrupt them.[1][4]

The winter campaign would determine how far the Red Army could turn survival into territorial recovery. That result was not yet known on 5 December. The achievement already established was immense: the Soviet state remained capable of fighting, and Germany faced a prolonged war beyond the assumptions of its invasion plan. For prisoners and occupied communities, prolonged war also meant continued danger. For Leningrad’s hungry residents, it meant another day in which food still had to arrive. The campaign closes here with the possibility of recovery preserved, the destruction already inflicted irreversible, and the fighting unfinished.[1][4]

chronologyNotes: 5 December is this atlas’s editorial endpoint, not a universally accepted formal termination date for Operation Barbarossa.
Account for verified Kalinin Front attacks on 5 December; the broader operations beginning on 6 December are context, not completed Phase V movements.
Tikhvin’s later recapture and the subsequent winter campaign must not be projected backward or opened as an empty new collection.
sourceMethod: Numbered notes connect the prose to specific inspected passages. The U.S. Army campaign history is a retrospective synthesis, assessed alongside Soviet documentary transcriptions, institutional accounts and scholarship. Guderian’s and German signals officers’ postwar explanations are attributed; their criticisms of higher command are not independent proof of their own conduct. Public Cambridge extracts, edited diary selections and catalogue-only evidence are identified in the locators. Russian and German material is paraphrased in English; uninspected archival originals are not claimed as consulted. Orders, reported implementation and independently established outcomes remain distinct. Operational analysis is Ostkrieg’s interpretation of the cited evidence. This local editorial revision does not validate or update the companion maps or their cached passages.
